flashcard_questions.a: An antibody from a single clone of cells that targets one specific antigen.

flashcard_questions.q: What is an antigen on a pathogen?
flashcard_questions.a: A molecule on its surface that triggers an immune response.

flashcard_questions.q: What is injected into a mouse to start monoclonal antibody production?
flashcard_questions.a: The specific antigen the antibodies must target.

flashcard_questions.q: Monoclonal antibody production: inject the antigen, extract ____, fuse them with ____ cells, then select and clone.

flashcard_questions.a: A cell made by fusing a lymphocyte with a tumour cell.

flashcard_questions.q: Why are tumour cells used to make hybridomas?
flashcard_questions.a: They divide rapidly and never stop dividing.

flashcard_questions.q: Why can lymphocytes not be used on their own to make antibodies in bulk?
flashcard_questions.a: Once they start producing antibodies they lose the ability to divide.

flashcard_questions.q: What is added to break down the cell membranes so the cells fuse?
Which hormone do pregnancy tests detect using monoclonal antibodies?
In which body fluid is HCG detected by a pregnancy test?
What does a pregnancy test strip show for a positive result?
What makes cancer cells a target for monoclonal antibodies?
flashcard_questions.a: They carry specific antigens on their surface that normal cells do not.

flashcard_questions.q: How can a monoclonal antibody kill a cancer cell directly?
flashcard_questions.a: It carries a radioactive substance or toxic drug straight to that cell.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does this treatment cause fewer side effects than traditional chemotherapy?
flashcard_questions.a: It targets only cancer cells, while chemotherapy kills all rapidly dividing cells.
